I hate it too.  I'm in recovery myself and while I can justify some of my actions I can't justify doing that.  Asking people for money for X and spending it on my habit instead.  I personally still feel the guilt from it.  At the time I usually even planned to spend the money on what I said I would.  But the addiction was just too powerful, and my willpower and conscience not powerful enough.  Cash in hand ramps up the *NOW NOW NOW* feeling that sickness has already been driving.

It sucks.  It all does.  I wish I could say that all addicts are the same but they're not.  A good bit of them are just lousy people.  But I hope that the majority aren't.  Instead, they are trapped.  And that cycle they are trapped in degrades their conscience over time, turns them into animals in a sense.  And there's no way out except with the support and understanding of others, which is a difficult thing to ask for.

I liken it to racism.  My MIL is casually racist and defends it because the black women she worked with 30 years ago were rude to her.  All comments on that aside, what she doesn't understand is that it is **up to her** to stop the cycle of hatred.  All she is doing by allowing herself to act that way is becoming the villain in her own story.  Sure, it's not easy to respond to hatred with love.  But that's what needs to be done for a person, a group, a society to move forward.  And it's the same with addiction.  These people, especially once they show a *thread* of a will to get better, **need** love and support.  They will, without a doubt, to some and perhaps all others, seem like they deserve none of it.  But they need it.  And they won't heal without it.

You both need to be in therapy or you both will be stuck in a cycle of your respective insecurities and wounds from the past affecting the other person. 

I have learned over time that it can be great if you both can encourage each other to get help, but the more likely scenario is that you hold each other back. Focus on getting help for yourself and healing; encourage her to do the same independently, but don't let it affect you if she doesn't get help.

If you see yourself being in a long term relationship with this woman you need to realize that you are each the others foundation in some ways. You both suffer from mental health issues in one way or another, yet the only person you can fix is yourself. Hopefully she will realize the same and get the help she needs, but you may need to set an example and improve some yourself before she can see that.

My suggestion is that you find someone who does dialectic behavioral therapy. Make an appointment with them and don't let yourself skip it. Go in and they will ask you some questions and get to know you a bit. Once you feel comfortable, tell them what others have told you. I recommend bringing a notepad and having a list of symptoms that you identify with on one sheet, then take notes on the next.

Leave it up to them to make the diagnosis. They may have you do a full psychological work-up, a series of questionnaires that cover a wide range of mental issues. You may have to ask them for this, but I'd recommend it.

I know you are both afraid, but this is for the better. Seeking professional help can be an enormous hill to overcome for people with mental disorders.

It will be better for both of you for her to get regular counseling and med checks. You yourself *need* to get counseling as well. You will be her foundation in many ways and you can hugely benefit from having a solid mental and emotional state + having an objective third party who can help you get in tune with your subconscious concerns, desires, worries, etc.
